verdicts.note: Transcript: 'a tremendous amount of my work is first person, because I think it's the natural storytelling voice' and later 'So to me, first person is the natural storytelling voice.' The home-recounting likeness is explicit: kid runs up asking 'What did you do today?' / 'How was school?' Every limb supported.

'If you're writing from the first person, if you are an assassin and you walk into the room and there's three people there, what he notices is going to be very different from the child character who runs in the room and is totally fixed on finding the toy they left there earlier.' 'Lost toy' = 'the toy they left there earlier'; both contrast limbs present.

'Why is she so pennypinching?' ... 'Charlotte grew up in a family with a very tight budget. So she always had to make choices. So this has affected her personality... All choices are very important and very dire for her.' Household-economy derivation and the consequential-choice limb both explicit.
'For me, the character has to be generated by the world. I don't think I could take a 21st century any person and believably insert them into a fantasy.' Both limbs verbatim.

'We're in an inn, and the serving boy is late coming... Whether that's even noticed or whether you're annoyed because somebody else is yelling at the serving boy or whether you're embarrassed or whether you quietly tip the kid.' All four listed reactions present in order.

Opening section: 'While many authors provide an interpretive frame through witnesses that highlights the hero's capabilities, Hobb places you inside Fitz's perspective and leaves you there.' The no-outside-witness limb rides on that contrastive clause (the essay denies the framing function of witnesses, not their existence -- it later cites others noticing him); read as 'no witness supplied to frame him', it is supported.

Section 'A Wild Soul': 'The difficulty in seeing Fitz clearly is that he almost never narrates his own power. He narrates his doubts, failures, grief, and shame.' Inference limb supported by 'His power and greatest gifts are invisible... and thus neither do we' plus 'always there, noticed by others and shaping the outcomes'.

Section 'A Master of His Craft': 'the training is still running beneath the surface constantly and automatically. When he enters Lant's room, within moments he has cataloged the medicinal unguents on the mantel, the two pens at the ready, the Stones puzzle on the table...' All three objects and the training framing present.

Section 'A Writer, Historian, and Chronicler of His Age': 'Fitz knew what official chroniclers could not' and 'He understands that history is not made only in councils and battles, but in bedrooms, kitchens, stables, sickrooms, and moments of private choice.' Source says Fitz 'knew' and 'records not only the public history... but his own place within it'; the records limb holds in substance.

Same section: 'His prose feels natural because it is intimate, but intimacy should not be mistaken for simplicity. The clarity with which he renders character, politics, landscape, memory, and moral conflict is itself evidence of extraordinary literary intelligence.' Both limbs verbatim, list matches exactly.
Opening section: 'She hides his magnificence in plain sight.' followed by 'Whether the reader sees past his harsh self-assessment is entirely up to the reader.' Both limbs verbatim.
